---
title: "The documents"
---

Before any of the stages make sense, it helps to have the cast in one place. A trial produces a
chain of documents and datasets, each written by different people, for different readers, at
different times. Most of the difficulty in what follows comes from the joins between them.

If you already work in one part of this chain, the useful thing here is probably the part you
don't touch.

## What a trial produces

| | What it is | Who writes it | What it fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Protocol** | The plan of the trial in prose: why, who, what happens to them, what is measured, what will be concluded | Clinical, medical, with statistical input | What the trial *is* |
| **SAP** | Statistical analysis plan. How the data will be analysed — populations, models, handling of missing data, the exact tables | Statistics | What "analysed" means |
| **CRF** | Case report form. The screens or pages a site fills in for each subject | Data management | What gets collected |
| **SDTM** | Study Data Tabulation Model. The collected data, standardised — one domain per kind of observation, close to what was recorded | Programming | What was observed |
| **ADaM** | Analysis Data Model. Datasets built *for* the analysis: one row per subject per parameter per visit, with derived values like change from baseline already computed | Programming | What is analysed |
| **TFL** | Tables, figures and listings — the output a reader of the study actually sees | Programming | What is reported |

The important thing about **SDTM and ADaM** being separate: SDTM is meant to faithfully record
what happened, and ADaM is meant to be analysis-ready. Change from baseline does not exist in
SDTM — someone has to decide which record *is* the baseline and subtract it. That decision is
made in a programming specification, written in prose, and it is exactly the kind of decision
this whole chain is trying to make explicit.

## Where the standards in this book sit

Three things are being applied on top of that chain, and they address different joins in it.

**ICH M11** is a template for the protocol itself. Fourteen sections, and in its electronic form
a list of data elements, each with a code — so a protocol stops being free prose and starts
being a structure that can be read by something other than a person. It addresses the protocol
alone.

**USDM** — the Unified Study Definition Model — is the protocol *as data*. Objectives,
endpoints, estimands, arms, populations, the schedule of activities, expressed as JSON against a
defined model. If M11 says what a protocol must contain, USDM is a shape that content can live
in and be queried from.

**AC/DC** — Analysis and Derivation Concepts — covers the other end: how a measurement becomes
an analysis result. Three kinds of thing:

- an **observation concept**, the atomic measured thing
- a **derivation concept**, a step that computes — select a baseline, subtract it, window a visit
- an **analysis concept**, the aggregated result — a comparison, a model, a summary

A **biomedical concept** sits underneath, as the standard definition of the thing being
measured: serum alanine aminotransferase, with its units, codes and permissible values.

Between them they cover the two ends and the join: M11 structures the sentence, USDM makes it
addressable, AC/DC declares what happens to the measurement. That is the path described in the
introduction — every step declared rather than implied — laid against the documents a trial
actually produces.

## The join this book is about

The study definition drives two things, not one. It says what will be *measured* — which becomes
a case report form, and through it the collected data — and it says what will be *concluded*,
which becomes the analysis. The two meet again at the end.

```
            protocol ──M11──▶ structured protocol ──USDM──▶ study as data
                                                                  │
              ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────┴──────────────┐
              │ schedule of activities:                objectives, endpoints,    │
              │ what is measured, and when             estimands: what is asked  │
              ▼                                                                  │
             CRF ──collection──▶ SDTM ──derivation──▶ ADaM                        │
                                                       │                         │
                                                       └──── AC/DC ◀─────────────┘
                                                                │
                                                                ▼
                                                            a result
```

The **CRF** sits on the left-hand branch: the schedule of activities says a subject has
chemistry taken at a given visit, and the case report form is where that becomes a field
somebody fills in. In the study definition, that link is already present — an activity names the
concepts it collects:

{{json:study/usdm/toriva-lung-301.usdm.json#study.versions[0].studyDesigns[0].activities[5].biomedicalConceptIds}}

That is the *Chemistry (LFTs, creatinine)* activity, naming five biomedical concepts.

This is where the biomedical concept earns its keep, and why it is worth understanding early:
**the same definition is supposed to govern both branches.** The concept that says what serum
alanine aminotransferase is — its units, its code, its permissible values — should determine the
field on the form, the variable in the collected data, and the thing the derivation binds to at
the far end. One definition, used at both ends, rather than a chain of people agreeing to mean
the same thing.

**This book walks the right-hand branch only.** It starts from analysis datasets that already
exist, and takes them to a result. The collection side — CRF design, and the path from a
completed form to standardised data — is a substantial subject in its own right and is not
exercised here. It is drawn because leaving it out makes the study definition look like an input
to analysis alone, which is the smaller half of what it is for.

The stages that follow walk the right-hand branch once, on one endpoint, and stop where the
declared analysis produces a number — then compare that number against what a programmer built
from the same plan by hand.

## A note on versions

All three standards are moving, and so is the tooling. This book describes:

- **ICH M11** in its merged electronic form, as mapped in the factory's `study/m11/`
- **USDM v4.0**
- CDISC's **analysis-concepts** repository at the commit this repository pins, which every
  screenshot here is stamped with

That is deliberate. A guide that claims to be current is wrong within a release; one that says
which version it describes stays useful, because you can tell what has moved since.
